name: Internal jugular vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
supplies_or_drains: drains the dural venous sinuses (intracranial, out of scope) plus most facial/lingual/pharyngeal/thyroid veins
notes: Descends in the carotid sheath alongside the common carotid artery and vagus nerve; joins subclavian_v_r (root of data/vascular/upper_limb_venous.json) posterior to the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein -- the same cross-file-seam documentation pattern used for the aortic arch in the arterial tree.

name: External jugular vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
supplies_or_drains: drains the scalp and posterior/superficial face
notes: Formed by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein; crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially (a visible surface landmark, especially when distended) before draining into subclavian_v_r.

name: Facial vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Runs a straighter course than its companion facial artery; valveless, giving it clinical significance for the spread of facial infection ('danger triangle' of the face, communicating with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins).

name: Retromandibular vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
supplies_or_drains: formed within the parotid gland from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins
notes: Splits into an anterior division (joins facial_v_r, draining ultimately to internal_jugular_v_r) and a posterior division (joins the posterior auricular vein to form external_jugular_v_r) -- modeled here under internal_jugular_v_r to represent the anterior-division pathway, with the posterior-division contribution to external_jugular_v_r documented rather than duplicated as a second parent (the same single-parent-tree simplification used for the ansa cervicalis loop in the nerve file).

name: Superficial temporal vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Maxillary vein (pterygoid plexus outflow)
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Drains the pterygoid venous plexus, a valveless network around the pterygoid muscles that also communicates with the cavernous sinus -- another route (with the facial vein) by which deep facial infection can spread intracranially.

name: Lingual vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Superior thyroid vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
supplies_or_drains: thyroid gland (out of scope as an organ, noted for completeness)

name: Occipital vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Drainage pattern is anatomically variable -- it may instead drain to the external jugular vein or directly to the suboccipital venous plexus/vertebral vein; parented here to internal_jugular_v_r as the most commonly cited pattern.

name: Posterior auricular vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Vertebral vein
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
notes: Formed from the suboccipital venous plexus, descends through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae (a documented bones.json landmark) alongside the vertebral artery, but -- unlike the artery -- drains directly into the brachiocephalic vein rather than joining the internal jugular system; modeled as its own root for the same cross-file-seam reason as internal/external jugular vein.

name: Anterior jugular vein
notes: Descends near the midline to drain into the external jugular or subclavian vein. Left and right are joined just above the sternum by the jugular venous arch, which bleeds briskly if divided during a low tracheostomy.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Pterygoid venous plexus
notes: Communicates with the cavernous sinus through emissary veins and with the facial vein through the deep facial vein. Because those communications are valveless, infection in the 'danger area' of the face can propagate backwards into the cavernous sinus.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Deep cervical vein
supplies_or_drains: suboccipital and deep posterior neck musculature
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Sigmoid sinus
supplies_or_drains: transverse sinus and the posterior cranial fossa
notes: S-shaped continuation of the transverse sinus, grooving the mastoid and becoming the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen. Its proximity to the mastoid air cells is why otitis media and mastoiditis can cause sigmoid sinus thrombosis.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Transverse sinus
supplies_or_drains: superior sagittal and straight sinuses, via the confluence of sinuses
notes: Usually asymmetric, the right being dominant in most people. That normal variant must not be read as thrombosis on imaging.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Superior sagittal sinus
supplies_or_drains: cerebrospinal fluid, via the arachnoid granulations
notes: Runs in the attached margin of the falx cerebri. Its arachnoid granulations return CSF to venous blood, which is why sagittal sinus thrombosis raises intracranial pressure.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Straight sinus
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Cavernous sinus
notes: Contains the internal carotid artery and CN VI within the sinus itself, with CN III, IV, V1 and V2 in its lateral wall. That packing explains the syndrome of cavernous sinus thrombosis: ophthalmoplegia, facial sensory loss in V1/V2 territory, proptosis and chemosis.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)
